A nonabelian Wilson surface on a lattice


Abstract
We analyze the nonabelian surface holonomy on a bipartite hypercubic lattice following a proposal in arXiv:1002.4636 [hep-th]. The bipartite structure of the lattice enables us to introduce spike string configurations. These spikes play a crucial role for the time evolution of the string when the total number of color indices changes.



Andreas Gustavsson

Physics Department, University of Seoul, Seoul 02504 KOREA

1
Introduction

The 6d
(2,0)
superconformal theory for the ADE series of possible gauge groups was first discovered in 1995 in
[
1
]
. Later a brane picture for the
A_{N-1}
series of gauge groups was presented with an M2 brane ending on a stack of M5 branes along a selfdual string in
[
2
]
. For an abelian gauge group, the worldvolume theory on an M5 brane is described by an abelian tensor multiplet that includes a two-form gauge potential
B
whose field strength
H=dB
is selfdual. Let us now consider
N+1
parallel M5 branes and let us separate one of these branes from a stack of
N
coincident M5 branes. This breaks the gauge group from
U(N+1)
down to
U(N)
. We imagine that this happens by a Higgs mechanism, but the precise details of such a Higgs mechanism are not known in six dimensions. From the brane perspective, we may have an M2 brane that stretches from the distant M5 to the stack of coincident M5 branes and it should be seen as a heavy selfdual string in the
U(N)
gauge theory that lives on the stack of coincident M5 branes. The selfdual string appears as a central charge in the supersymmetry algebra of the M5 brane theory. We can partially understand this for a nonabelian gauge group since the supersymmetry algebra itself makes no reference to the gauge group, although if the gauge group is nonabelian, we do not have an explicit realization of these central charges. From this algebra and its central charge that corresponds to the selfdual strings, one may argue that two parallel selfdual strings shall be BPS saturated and that there shall be a zero net force between them. The BPS nature of two parallel selfdual strings was also shown explicitly for an abelian tensor multiplet minimally coupled to an effective action for the two selfdual strings in
[
3
]
, where it was shown that for two parallel selfdual strings there is an electromagnetic repulsion force that cancels the Higgs field attraction force. If on the other hand, we have two anti-parallel selfdual strings, then this system is unstable and we expect that the two strings will come together and annihilate into electromagnetic radiation. The net electric and magnetic charges for this system is vanishing, which makes it consistent for the two strings to annihilate into charge neutral radiation particles. We expect that a closed selfdual string will behave in a similar way so that it will shrink and annihilate itself into radiation, unless there is an obstruction that stabilizes it. If there is a circle direction in the manifold, then the string will stabilize at the radius of the circle direction. Such a closed string will be perceived as a charged particle under dimensional reduction around the circle. Dimensional reduction of the selfdual string as it wraps either of the one-cycles of a two-torus was used to explain electric-magnetic duality in abelian four-dimensional Maxwell theory in
[
4
]
.

For an abelian two-form gauge potential we have an associated gauge invariant Wilson surface for any closed two-dimensional smooth surface. Its expectation value is a measurable real number, which, depending on the geometry, can be either an observable or a Weyl anomaly
[
5
]
,
[
6
]
. On the other hand, a surface that has a boundary is not gauge invariant. However, Wilson surfaces with boundaries that we will refer to as surface holonomies, are important when we couple them to selfdual strings. The question that we will address is how the surface holonomy acts on a heavy string as it moves adiabatically. In order to simplify the analysis, we will not consider selfdual strings with equal magnetic and electric charges. Instead we will consider an electrically charged heavy string with a vanishing magnetic charge. We treat this string as a first quantized string that we describe by a Schrodinger wave function. The question that we will address is how the nonabelian surface holonomy acts on this string wave function under parallel transportation. To this end, we need to understand how to define a nonabelian surface holonomy.

A proposal for a nonabelian Wilson surface on a hypercubic lattice was presented in
[
7
]
, which was furher studied in
[
8
]
. However, this construction of a nonabelian Wilson surface on a hypercubic lattice dates back already to the early ’80s where it first appeared in
[
9
]
. See also
[
10
]
,
[
11
]
,
[
12
]
for related works around that time. In this paper we will apply this proposal and show that the surface holonomy can transport a heavy electrically charged string across the lattice in a consistent manner. This will enable us to obtain the unitary compactness condition the surface holonomy shall satisfy. We will also show that the surface holonomy on a plaquette has a unit element up to a gauge transformation.

2
From
U(1)
to
U(N)
higher gauge theory

Let us consider Maxwell theory on
\mathbb{R}^{1,5}
of a two-form gauge potential
B
with field strength
H=dB
. In this theory we may have an electric string with tension
T
and electric charge
e
. The action for this system is a sum

\displaystyle S

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle S_{Maxwell}+S_{string}

(2.1)

where
S_{string}=S_{NG}+S_{B}
are given by

\displaystyle S_{Maxwell}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle-\frac{1}{12}\int d^{6}xH_{MNP}H^{MNP}

(2.2)

\displaystyle S_{NG}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle-T\int_{\Sigma}d^{2}\sigma\sqrt{-g}

(2.3)

\displaystyle S_{B}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle e\int_{\Sigma}B

(2.4)

respectively. Here
-g>0
is minus of the determinant of the induced metric on the string worldsheet
\Sigma
in Lorentzian signature. The two-form gauge potential is integrated over
\Sigma
in a metric independent way.

For a nearly straight string we may describe small fluctuations around it by choosing static gauge

\displaystyle X^{0}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle t

(2.5)

\displaystyle X^{5}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle s

(2.6)

\displaystyle X^{i}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\xi^{i}(t,s)

(2.7)

and expanding in powers of the small fluctuation
\xi^{i}
. To lowest order we get

\displaystyle S_{string}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{T}{2}\int dtds\left(\dot{\xi}^{2}-\xi^{\prime 2}\right)+e\int dtdsB_{ts}(t,x,\xi(t,s))

(2.8)

The Hamiltonian is

\displaystyle H

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\int ds\left(-\frac{1}{2T}\frac{\delta^{2}}{\delta\xi^{i}(s)\delta\xi^{i}(s)}+\frac{T}{2}\xi^{\prime}(s)^{2}\right)-e\int dsB_{ts}

(2.9)

The Schrodinger equation is

\displaystyle i\hbar\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial t}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle H\psi

(2.10)

If we assume that the string moves adiabatically
1
1

1

One way that we may move the string adiabatically is by letting it be static and just letting it evolve in time. Another way is may take
T
to infinity and move the string as a rigid string.
, then we solve this equation as

\displaystyle\psi(t_{2})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle e^{\frac{ie}{\hbar}\int_{t_{1}}^{t_{2}}\int dsB_{ts}}\psi(t_{1})

(2.11)

We then elevate this argument to a general claim that upon quantization, the Schrodinger wave function of this string changes by a phase factor as

\displaystyle\psi(C)

\displaystyle\rightarrow

\displaystyle\psi(C^{\prime})=U(\Sigma)\psi(C)

(2.12)

if we move the string adiabatically from the initial curve
C
to the final curve
C^{\prime}
along the surface
\Sigma
where the phase factor

\displaystyle U(\Sigma)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle e^{\frac{ie}{\hbar}\int_{\Sigma}B}

(2.13)

is the surface holonomy valued in the
U(1)
gauge group, satisfying the compactness condition

\displaystyle U(\Sigma)^{*}U(\Sigma)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle 1

(2.14)

as follows from that
B
is real. This claim can be understood by a path integral argument where the wave function changes by the phase factor
e^{\frac{i}{\hbar}S_{B}}
if we assume that adiabatic motion means that we can neglect the contribution from
S_{NG}
. From now on, we will put
\hbar=1
by a choice of natural units.

Under a
U(1)
gauge transformation

\displaystyle B\rightarrow B+d\Lambda

(2.15)

the surface holonomy transforms as

\displaystyle U(\Sigma)\rightarrow g(\partial\Sigma)U(\Sigma)

(2.16)

where the
U(1)
gauge group element
g(\partial\Sigma)
is evaluated on the boundary
\partial\Sigma
of the surface
\Sigma
and is given by

\displaystyle g(\partial\Sigma)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle e^{ie\int_{\partial\Sigma}\Lambda}

(2.17)

If
\Sigma
has the boundary given by two loops
C^{\prime}
and
C
, then

\displaystyle g(\partial\Sigma)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle e^{ie\left(\int_{C^{\prime}}\Lambda-\int_{C}\Lambda\right)}

(2.18)

that we may also write as

\displaystyle g(\partial\Sigma)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle g(C^{\prime})\left(g(C)\right)^{*}

(2.19)

where

\displaystyle g(C)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle e^{ie\int_{C}\Lambda}

(2.20)

The sign factors that appear in these two boundary integrals is important, so let us explain it in detail. On the surface
\Sigma
we have an intrinsic orientation that we may represent by drawing small circles everywhere on the surface, each circle has its own orientation. We determine the orientation of nearby circles so that any two circles that meet tangentially at any point has opposite tangential directions. This means that once we decide the orientation of just one small circle, the orientation of all the other circles in
\Sigma
is uniquely fixed. This collection of oriented small circles is what we may call as the orientation of
\Sigma
. Now we shall imagine the boundary circle
C^{\prime}
being connected tangentially to a small circle in
\Sigma
with a tangential direction that is parallel to the tangent direction of
C^{\prime}
. Then that small circle in turn is connected to another small circle in
\Sigma
tangentially so that their tangents point in opposite directions and this will continue with many small circles all the way down to
C
. Then the circle that is tangential to
C
will have a tangential direction that is anti-parallel to the tangential direction of
C
. That is the explanation for why we have a relative minus sign between the two integrals. We may summarize this long text by writing it as a compact formula,

\displaystyle\partial\Sigma

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle C^{\prime}\cup C^{\vee}

(2.21)

where
C^{\vee}
denotes the loop
C
with its orientation reversed. We draw the surface and its two boundary loops below,

C^{\prime}
C
\Sigma

(2.22)

The wave function needs to also transform under the gauge transformation as

\displaystyle\psi(C^{\prime})

\displaystyle\rightarrow

\displaystyle g(C^{\prime})\psi(C^{\prime})

(2.23)

\displaystyle\psi(C)

\displaystyle\rightarrow

\displaystyle g(C)\psi(C)

(2.24)

while the surface holonomy transforms as

\displaystyle U(\Sigma)

\displaystyle\rightarrow

\displaystyle g(C^{\prime})U(\Sigma)\left(g(C)\right)^{*}

(2.25)

in order to ensure that the transport of the string by the surface holonomy as given by equation (
2.12
), is gauge covariant. Let us now consider the case when
C^{\prime}
approaches
C
so that the area of
\Sigma
shrinks to zero when
C^{\prime}
is on top of
C
. Let us denote this degenerate surface as
\Sigma_{0}
. For such a degenerate surface, the surface holonomy becomes gauge invariant,

\displaystyle U(\Sigma_{0})\rightarrow g(C)U(\Sigma_{0})\left(g(C)\right)^{*}=U(\Sigma_{0})

(2.26)

We state this rather trivial observation here because it turns out to be important as we turn to the nonabelian generalization.

If we parametrize the closed string as
s\to C^{M}(s)
for
s\sim s+2\pi
, then the gauge covariant differential of the wave function is given by

\displaystyle D\psi(C)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\int ds\delta C^{M}(s)\left(\frac{\delta\psi(C)}{\delta C^{M}(s)}-ieB_{MN}(C(s))\frac{dC^{N}(s)}{ds}\psi(C)\right)

(2.27)

By taking the complex conjugate, we get

\displaystyle\left(D\psi(C)\right)^{*}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\int ds\delta C^{M}(s)\left(\frac{\delta\psi(C)^{*}}{\delta C^{M}(s)}+ieB_{MN}(C(s))\frac{d{C}^{N}(s)}{ds}\psi(C)^{*}\right)

(2.28)

The same operator on the righ-hand side is obtained if we change the orientation of the string such that
\dot{C}^{M}(s)
is replaced by
-\dot{C}^{M}(s)
,

\displaystyle D\widetilde{\psi}(C^{\vee})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\int ds\delta C^{M}(s)\left(\frac{\delta\widetilde{\psi}(C^{\vee})}{\delta C^{M}(s)}+ieB_{MN}(C(s))\frac{d{C}^{N}(s)}{ds}\widetilde{\psi}(C^{\vee})\right)

(2.29)

Here
\widetilde{\psi}(C^{\vee})
is another wave function that is evaluated on
C^{\vee}
, the string whose orientation is reversed compared to
C
. We can now gauge covariantly equate these two wave functions as

\displaystyle\psi(C)^{*}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\widetilde{\psi}(C^{\vee})

(2.30)

Another way to argue for this relation comes from the complex conjugation relations

\displaystyle\psi(C^{\prime})^{*}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle U(\Sigma)^{*}\psi(C)^{*}

(2.31)

\displaystyle U(\Sigma)^{*}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle U(\Sigma^{\vee})

(2.32)

Here
\Sigma^{\vee}
is the surface
\Sigma
with its orientation reversed. For the boundaries, we have

\displaystyle\partial\Sigma

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle C^{\prime}\cup C^{\vee}

(2.33)

\displaystyle\partial\Sigma^{\vee}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle C^{\prime\vee}\cup C^{\vee}

(2.34)

Now since
C^{\vee}
is just another closed curve, we shall also have

\displaystyle\widetilde{\psi}(C^{\prime\vee})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle U(\Sigma^{\vee})\widetilde{\psi}(C^{\vee})

(2.35)

In this way we again see that we may write a covariant relation as

\displaystyle\psi(C)^{*}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\widetilde{\psi}(C^{\vee})

(2.36)

Below we illustrate this relation for
\Sigma
a cylinder,

\displaystyle\left(\vbox{\hbox{

(2.37)

Let us now consider a spacetime where one direction is circle compactified. Then we may consider a sitution where our cylinder is extended in time and wraps around the circle direction in space. If we then perform dimensional reduction along the circle direction, the cylinder
\Sigma
connecting the two circles
C
and
C^{\prime}
will reduce to a line
\gamma
connecting two endpoints
x
and
x^{\prime}
. On this dimensionally reduced line holonomy, complex conjugation acts as drawn below,

(2.38)

This graphical relation shows that the line holonomy satisfies

\displaystyle\left(U(\gamma)\right)^{*}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle U(\gamma^{\vee})

(2.39)

where
\gamma^{\vee}
denotes the line with its orientation reversed. The gauge group was assumed to be abelian, but for the line holonomy this has a natural generalization to
U(N)
gauge group where the relation becomes

\displaystyle\left(U^{i^{\prime}}{}_{i}(\gamma)\right)^{*}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle U^{i}{}_{i^{\prime}}(\gamma^{\vee})

(2.40)

(2.42)

However, if we place only one color index on each string, then it is difficult to understand what shall happen to that index if the string splits into two strings,
2
2

2

If we have a flat line holonomy, then we may use that to parallel transport the color index
j
from a basepoint to any other point. However, this does not apply to the M5 brane theory where we do not have a line holonomy, flat or not. Namely, suppose that we had such a line holonomy. Then we would also have a Wilson loop observable. But there is no such observable in the abelian M5 brane theory. Since the loop itself is a geometric object, it exists independently of the choice of gauge group and so it follows that we do not have a line holonomy in the nonabelian generalization either.

i^{\prime}
???
i

(2.43)

But in the
U(1)
gauge theory we can have a surface holonomy that describes a string splitting process. Every quantity that is involved in such a string splitting process is well-defined. The surface holonomy on such a worldsheet is well-defined as we just need to integrate the two-form
B
over it. For the gauge parameter, we may write it as

\displaystyle g(C)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle e^{ie\int_{0}^{2\pi}ds\Lambda_{M}(C(s))\dot{C}^{M}(s)}

(2.44)

for the string just the moment before it splits, and as

\displaystyle g(C)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle e^{ie\int_{0}^{a}ds\Lambda_{M}(C(s))\dot{C}^{M}(s)}e^{ie\int_{a}^{2\pi}ds\Lambda_{M}(C(s))\dot{C}^{M}(s)\dot{C}^{M}(s)}

(2.45)

the moment after the string has split into two strings. Here the string splits after the string develops a self-intersection point at parameter value
a\in(0,2\pi)
where

\displaystyle C^{M}(a)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle C^{M}(0)

(2.46)

The string splitting process can be iterated indefinitely by dividing the original parameter interval
[0,2\pi]
into smaller and smaller sub-intervals repeatedly. That this is possible stems from the uncountable nature of the number of points in the interval
[0,2\pi]
so that no matter how short we make a sub-interval, it still contains just as many points as the original interval.

For the generalization to
U(N)
gauge group, and if we put only one color index on each string,

j
k
i

(2.47)

then the surface holonomy will be a map from a wave function with one color index
i
, to a wave function describing two disjoint strings, each with one color index
j
and
k
respectively. It seems difficult to understand how that can be described by a unitary process.

If instead we put two color indices
i
and
j
on the incoming string, then we can preserve the total number of color indices if we put one color index on each outgoing string,

k
{{\ell}}
i,j

(2.48)

Such a process corresponds to a surface holonomy that takes two incoming color indices
i
and
j
and transforms them into two outgoing color indices
k
and
{{\ell}}
. Since we have equal numbers of color indices incoming as outgoing, we can describe this process with a unitary matrix. But the surface does not necessarily have to be a worldsheet surface that extends in time. It can also be a surface that is located at an instant in time and extends in spatial directions. Alternatively, we may Wick rotate the time direction so that all directions are spatial. In such a situation there is no invariant way to tell what will be an incoming and what will be an outgoing closed string. The same process can be viewed as if the string with the color index
k
is incoming and splits into two strings, each with color indices
i,j
and
{{\ell}}
respectively and then it is difficult to see how such a process can be unitary.

There now seems to be only two possibilities to achieve a unitary development. Either we have an abelian gauge group and a surface holonomy carries no color indices, or else if the gauge group is nonabelian, and we will assume a
U(N)
gauge group, then we need an infinite number of color indices that are associated to each string. In both cases, we then have the property that a string can be split into two strings in an indefinite sequence of iterated processes. Importantly, this possibility of having an indefinite iterating sequence of string splitting arises as a result of having an uncountable infinite set of color indices and of points in the parameter interval
[0,2\pi]
. Here we thus start to see a possible connection between spacetime points and color indices.

3
From uncountable to countable

If spacetime is a continuum, then it seems like we need an uncountable number of color indices to decorate the string. However, even in the continuum of spacetime and a smooth string, that infinity should be possible to coarse-grain.

Let us start by looking at the loop algebra associated to the gauge group
U(N)
. The loop algebra generators will be denoted
t_{a}(s)
. They satisfy the Lie algebra

\displaystyle[t_{a}(s),t_{b}(s^{\prime})]

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle if_{ab}{}^{c}\delta(s-s^{\prime})t_{c}(s)

(3.1)

where
f_{ab}{}^{c}
are the structure constants of
U(N)
. The zero modes,

\displaystyle t_{a}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\int_{0}^{2\pi}dst_{a}(s)

(3.2)

are the reparametrization invariant generators of
U(N)
. The loop algebra generators have the nice property that they can easily handle a string the splits into two strings. If the string splits at
s=a

where
a
is a number in the range
0<a<2\pi
, then the generators
\{t_{a}(s)|0\leq s\leq a\}
will act only on the first string and the generators
\{t_{a}(s)|a\leq s\leq 2\pi\}
will act only on the second string and the generators from differents sets commute. Generators within each set form separate loop algebras. One might worry that a contact term could arise from the common point
s=a
. But the following argument shows that no contact term will arise there. Let us view the generators as maps from the space of continuous functions on the circle into the loop algebra,

\displaystyle t_{a}[f]

\displaystyle:=

\displaystyle\int_{0}^{2\pi}dst_{a}(s)f(s)

(3.3)

The loop algebra is given by

\displaystyle[t_{a}[f],t_{b}[g]]

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle if_{ab}{}^{c}t_{c}[fg]

(3.4)

From this result it immediately follows that if
f
has its support in
[0,a]
, that is, on the first string, and
g
has its support in
[a,2\pi]
, that is, on the second string, then
fg
vanishes in the entire interval
[0,2\pi]
for continuous functions
f
and
g
, so the two sets of generators commute. Within each string, we now have got an inherited loop algebra. Thus from a single parent loop algebra, we see that we can generate two children loop algebras that commute with each other and who live on each string separately. This process can be iterated indefinitely by dividing the interval
[0,2\pi]
into smaller and smaller peaces and there is no limit on how finely we can divide this interval, the key point being that no matter how ’small’ an interval is, it will still contain just as many ’points’ as the original interval did. That is, an uncountable infinite number of points.

Let us now consider a closed string and divide it into
n
intervals
I_{m}=[a_{m-1},a_{m}]
with
a_{0}=0
and
0<a_{1}<a_{2}<...<a_{n-1}<2\pi
. We associate with the interval
I_{m}
a wave function
\psi^{i}_{m}
. Here
i=1,...,N
is a fundamental index of
U(N)
. The wave function of the whole string is the product

\displaystyle\psi^{i_{n}\cdots i_{1}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\psi^{i_{n}}_{n}\cdots\psi^{i_{1}}_{1}

(3.5)

in a simplified notation, as later we will see that half the color indices are anti-fundamentals indices that we shall put downstairs. Here we will ignore this detail though. We then define

\displaystyle t_{a}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\sum_{m=0}^{n-1}(t_{a})^{i}{}_{j}\psi^{j}_{m}\frac{\partial}{\partial\psi^{i}_{m}}

(3.6)

that act on the string wave function as

\displaystyle t_{a}\psi^{i_{n}\cdots i_{1}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\sum_{m=0}^{n-1}(t_{a})^{i_{m}}{}_{j_{m}}\psi^{i_{n}\cdots i_{m-1}j_{m}i_{m+1}\cdots i_{1}}

(3.7)

These generators can be obtained from a continuum limit that is given by the loop algebra. In the continuum limit we replace the coarse-grained wave functions
\psi^{i}_{m}
on each interval on the string with
\psi^{i}(s)
at each point of the string. We then define the action of the loop algebra generators at each point of the string as

\displaystyle t_{a}(s)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle(t_{a})^{i}{}_{j}\psi^{j}(s)\frac{\delta}{\delta\psi^{i}(s)}

(3.8)

We then get back the above coarse-grained system from the continuum string by restricting the wave function to be stepwise constant on each interval,

\displaystyle\psi^{i}(s)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\psi^{i}_{m}\qquad\mbox{for}\qquad s\in I_{m}

(3.9)

It is not clear to us how to write the wave function of the entire string in the continuum limit. We do not have the proper continuum version of (
3.5
). Intuitively this would be an uncountably infinite product of wave functions

\displaystyle"\Pi_{s\in[0,2\pi]}\psi^{i(s)}(s)"

(3.10)

The difficulty in understanding the continuum limit of the wave function of the string is what motivates us to study a lattice regularization.

The wave function of the string may carry several color indices
i,j,k,...
and we do not assume any additional structure for these color indices, such as that they form an adjoint representation of the gauge group. Instead, we will assume that the wave function transforms in the highly reducible representation

\displaystyle N\otimes\bar{N}\otimes N\otimes\bar{N}\otimes N\cdots\otimes\bar{N}

(3.11)

This suggests that a continuum limit either does not exist, or if it does exist, then it will require us to development a representation theory that goes far beyond simple loop algebras that can deal with truly infinite-dimensional representations of the
U(N)
gauge group.

4
The hexeract

We will take the lattice to be bipartite and densily packed with six-dimensional cubes, called ’hexeracts’. As far as surface holonomies concern, we do not need a metric and only the topological structure of the lattice will be important. Since the hexeracts is in higher dimensions, let us start with something that we can visualize, namely the three-dimensional cube. Below we will draw the cube in such a way that its graph can be generalized to higher dimensions,

(000)
(001)
(010)
(100)
(011)
(101)
(110)
(111)

(4.1)

With just a small amount of imagination we can easily see the cube as an embedding in three dimensions from the above two-dimensional graph. But the two-dimensional graph itself can be generalized to any higher dimensions. In higher dimensions our ability to visualize gets lost since we can not visualize objects in higher dimensions. But we can still draw the graphs. For example, the graph below captures the topology of a four-dimensional cube (4-cube or tesseract). We have highlighted two of its eight 3-cubes in red and blue colors respectively. These are located at vertices
(abc0)
and
(abc1)
, with
a,b,c=0,1
, respectively,

(0000)
(0001)
(0010)
(0100)
(1000)
(0011)
(0101)
(1001)
(0110)
(1010)
(1100)
(0111)
(1011)
(1101)
(1110)
(1111)

(4.2)

There are eight
3
-cubes in the
4
-cube in total. They correspond to the number of ways we pick the vertices that form a cube. To obtain these vertices, we need to first select one slot among four entries and in that slot insert either 0 or 1. This leads to

\displaystyle 8

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\binom{4}{1}2

(4.3)

possibilies. This result generalizes to an
n
-cube for which we have the following number of
k
-cubes,

\displaystyle\binom{n}{k}2^{n-k}

(4.4)

This formula is valid for
k=0,1,...,n
. One may check that the number of
0
-cubes are the
2^{n}
number of vertices, and the number of
n
-cubes is equal to one.

We are now specifically interested in the hypercubic lattice whose building blocks are hexeracts. The topological structure of the hexeract is drawn below,

The hexeract has 64 vertices that are connected in certain ways by 192 edges so that each vertex connects to six other vertices of the opposite type (white or black). These edges form 240 plaquettes (2-cubes), 160 cubes (3-cubes), 60 tesseracts (4-cubes), and 12 penteracts (5-cubes).

If we stretch out the above net of lines in all six Euclidean dimensions then we get a regular hexeract. This is a very simple object if one looks at it from afar along anyone of the six Euclidean coordinate directions. One will then see only one plaquette of the hexeract. There are in total
\binom{6}{2}=15
coordinate planes in which this plaquette can be extended. We also need to specify if that is seen from the top or from the bottom in the given transverse direction. Since there are four transverse direction to anyone of the planes, there are in total
16
different ways to assign tops and bottoms in each of those four directions. In total there are therefore
240
different plaquettes of the hexeract that we may see by looking at this object from afar. If then we were to rotate the hexeract a little bit in our view, then we will see a tremendous complexity arises from this single plaquette, and it may appear to us in a shape similar to what is drawn above.

5
Coloring the lattice

The hypercubic lattice built with hexeracts has a bipartite structure where each white vertex is connected to twelve black vertices by twelve edges and each black vertex is connected by twelve edges to twelve white vertices. We put one color index
i,j,k,{{\ell}},m,....=1,...,N
on each edge in this lattice. In this way, each edge gets the name of the index we put there. The most important structure in this lattice for string dynamics is the plaquette. When the string moves, a segment of the string has to cross some plaquette, regardless of how the string moves. The plaquette has one face, four edges and four vertices,

{{\ell}}
k
j
i

(5.1)

A string in this lattice goes along the edges in the lattice. We define a ’segment’ of the string as a portion of that string that goes along exactly one edge in the lattice.

A string that stretches over edges in the lattice, will cross vertices of different type interchangingly each time. We will associate one color index
i,j,k,...
of the wave function of the string to each edge that the string stretches over. If the gauge group is
U(N)
then
i=1,...,N
and for
N>2
we have two distinct
N
-dimensional representations, the fundamental
\psi^{i}
and the anti-fundamental
\psi_{i}
representation.
3
3

3

For
N=2
we may still place the indices upstairs and downstairs, although in that case there is an invariant antisymmetric tensor
{\cal{\varepsilon}}_{ij}
relating them. For
SO(N)
gauge group the string is unoriented and we shall not distinguish between indices upstairs or downstairs. One way to see that the strings are unoriented is by recalling that for the D4 branes an
SO(N)
gauge group arise from unoriented strings ending on these D4 branes. These strings originate correspond to unoriented M2 branes wrapping the M-theory circle. We conclude that the selfdual strings must be unoriented since they are the boundaries of these unoriented M2 branes.
The string has an orientation, for
U(N)
gauge group, which enables us to decide whether a color index shall be fundamental or anti-fundamental from the geometry of the string on the lattice. We use the convention that if the arrow of the string points away from a white vertex of the lattice then we put the color index upstairs and otherwise downstairs. We will write these color indices reading from the right to the left as we go along the string in the direction of its orientation or its arrow direction. The color indices are indices associated to the string. But we find it convenient to put the color indices on all the edges of the lattice. This makes the indices act not only as internal indices of the gauge group, but also as geometrical markers for where the string is located. As the string moves over the lattice, the indices on the string will change so that the string picks up the indices from the edges of the lattice over which it stretches. Given a geometric view of the color indices as describing the entire string, we only need to read the color indices as we go along the string to specify its geometric shape in the lattice. Below we show a string on the lattice with three different color indices whose wave function is written by our set of conventions as
\psi^{k}{}_{j}{}^{i}
,

i
j
k

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\psi^{k}{}_{j}{}^{i}

(5.2)

We will now motivate why we shall put the color indices in their conjugate representations as we go along the string following the lattice bipartite structure.

As we put a closed string on a lattice, it may happen that the string self-intersects in various ways. For example, it may happen that two different segments of the string come together and run along the same edge on the lattice. We are now interesteed in the case when they are antiparallel on that edge and in particular we will study a situation where the string makes a spike-move as depicted below,

i
j
k

\longrightarrow

i
k
k^{\prime}
j
x

(5.3)

Under this spike-move the string acquires two new segments that are anti-parallel along the spike. Accordingly, the wave function gets two new color indices. If the lattice edge is labeled
k
, then as the spike is created, the first string segment will pick up the color index
k
and the second string segment on that edge will get the color index
k^{\prime}
. Under the spike-move the wave function transforms as

\displaystyle\psi_{j}{}^{i}\rightarrow\psi_{j}{}^{k^{\prime}}{}_{k}{}^{i}

(5.4)

Let us now try to deduce what the transformed wave function shall be, in a more detailed form. Let us first consider an abelian Wilson surface, the surface that is generated by time translation for the string that has a spike. This surface will have an infinitesimally narrow crease, which is the spike translated in time. The abelian Wilson surface has a crease-cross symmetry, by which we mean the uplift to the surface of the zig-zag symmetry that we have for a Wilson line.
4
4

4

The zig-zag symmetry might have lost some of its original popularity after it was realized that the gravity dual leads to a Wilson loop with a scalar field in the loop as such a Maldacena-Wilson loop does not have the zig-zag symmetry. We do not consider a coupling to a scalar field and all our Wilson surfaces, abelian as well as nonabelian, have the crease-cross symmetry.
The integrals of the two-form gauge potential over the two sheets of the infinitesimally narrow crease cancel out. In abelian two-form gauge theory, the surface holonomy that deforms a string into a spike is therefore the identity transformation.

We propose that the nonabelian generalization should be obtained by replacing the identity operator with the Kroenecker delta
\delta^{k^{\prime}}_{k}
up to a normalization factor. This is a gauge invariant tensor of
U(N)
and it is natural to have a gauge invariant tensor associated with a spike deformation of the string since this deformation does not cover any surface area.

The structure of this invariant tensor – the Kroenecker delta – with one fundamental index upstairs and one anti-fundamental index downstairs for the two oppositely oriented string segments on the edge of the spike, is the reason why we shall place the color indices on the string wave function upstairs and downstairs according to the bipartite structure of the lattice. The spike wave function will now get the correct index structure enabling us to incorporate the spike portion in the string wave function as

\displaystyle\psi_{j}{}^{k^{\prime}}{}_{k}{}^{i}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle c\delta_{k}^{k^{\prime}}\psi_{j}{}^{i}

(5.5)

where
c
is a normalization constant that we will fix shortly.

We assume that the string is a first quantized heavy string and the wave function that describes it is a Schrodinger wave function. When two massive segments of the string meet and annihilate into massless charge-neutral particles, they escape from the string. These massless particles can not be described by the nonrelativistic wave function of our string. From the perspective of the wave function, that means that we have to allow for it to either lose old and acquire new color indices when spikes are created or annihilated by processes that fall the framework of nonrelativistic quantum mechanics.

By extracting the coefficient of
c\delta_{k}^{k^{\prime}}
we get a wave function that has two color indices less. This corresponds to a string where the spike is not present anymore.

Below we draw a two-segmented closed string. Such a string can shrink to either the vertex
x
or to the vertex
y
,

\displaystyle\psi^{k}{}_{k}=c\psi(x)=c\psi(y)

\psi(x)=\psi(y)
carries no color index. The string gets localized at a vertex in the lattice. In particular, a pointlike string can move over the lattice as a charge-neutral object without acquiring a surface holonomy, as long as it moves adiabatically and without expanding beyond a spike-string configuration as it moves.

In this case, its wave function vanishes,

\displaystyle\psi^{k}{}_{k^{\prime}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle 0

(5.11)

signaling that this string configuration does not exist, or that it exists with zero probabiliity.

Let us break
U(N)
gauge group down to
\Pi_{i=1}^{N}U(1)_{i}
by slightly separating all the
N
M5-branes. Let us consider an M2 brane that is stretching from the distant M5 brane to the
i
-th M5 brane (where
i=1,...,N
). The interpretation of the wave function
\psi^{k}{}_{k^{\prime}}=c\delta^{k}_{k^{\prime}}\psi
is now more clear. Its norm square
|\psi^{k}{}_{k^{\prime}}|^{2}=c^{2}\delta^{k}_{k^{\prime}}|\psi|^{2}
gives the probability for the first M2 brane to stretch from the distant M5 brane to the
k
-th M5 brane and the second M2 brane to stretch to the
k^{\prime}
-th M5 brane. If
k^{\prime}
is different from
k
, and if the first string carries
U(1)_{k}
electric charge
+e
then the other string will carry
U(1)_{k}
charge zero, whereas it carries
U(1)_{k^{\prime}}
charge
-e
. These electric charges do not cancel, neither with respect to
U(1)_{k}
nor with respect to
U(1)_{k^{\prime}}
. Therefore a string with these electric charges can not be deformed to a charge-neutral pointlike string. The wave function being zero for
k
and
k^{\prime}
different means that we do not have a string with
k
and
k^{\prime}
different from each other that can be deformed into a charge-neutral particle.

If two string segments meet on an edge where they have the same orientation then nothing special happens. Two straight infinitely extended parallel selfdual strings that are parallel remain BPS saturated at any distance (including zero distance) and the configuration is stable. While we do not assume that our strings are selfdual, since there is no invariant tensor of the form
\delta_{kk^{\prime}}
in
U(N)
gauge group for
N>2
, we are nevertheless led to assume that nothing particular happens to the wave function if two segments meet on one edge and if the two segments are parallel. All we need to do, is to put a prime on the second string segment landing on the edge
k
. So the first string segment gets color index
k
and the second string segment gets color index
k^{\prime}
there.

Let us now consider an example where the string moves across a plaquette by a move that we will refer to as the
3\to 1
move. As we will explain in more detail later, on this plaquette there lives a cyclically symmetric universal plaquette holonomy
U_{i}{}^{j}{}_{k}{}^{{{\ell}}}
that governs how the wave function of any string is affected when it moves across the plaquette. Now let us consider a string that moves across this plaquette as drawn below,

\displaystyle\begin{array}[]{ccccc}\vbox{\hbox{\hbox to108.5pt{\vbox to113.73pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 11.0327pt\lower-14.01126pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}
{}{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\hbox{\hbox{{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {{}{{}}{}{}}
\lxSVG@closescope }}}
{}{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\hbox{\hbox{{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {{}{{}}{}{}}
\lxSVG@closescope }}}

The wave function of the string under these moves transforms as

\displaystyle\psi^{k}{}_{j}{}^{i}

\displaystyle\overset{\text{$2\to 2$ move}}{\longrightarrow}

\displaystyle U^{{{\ell}}}{}_{i^{\prime}}{}^{j}{}_{k}\psi^{k}{}_{j}{}^{i}=c\psi^{{{\ell}}}\delta^{i}_{i^{\prime}}

(5.14)

\displaystyle\overset{\text{R-move}}{\longrightarrow}

\displaystyle\psi^{{{\ell}}}

(5.15)

We adopt the Einstein summation convention when two color indices appear twice with one upstairs and the other downstairs.

In the last transformation, we describe the annihilation of the spike by removing the Kroenecker delta from the wave function by a move that we will call the R-move.

The spike adds a mass to the string and the string wants to reach a lower energy state. So a spike will decay, and if the string is static otherwise, then we will get the same string without the spike. However, we will assume that when the string has got a spike, then it will not disappear instantaneously. The time delay means that there is a time window when we can pull the two string segments apart before their charges neutralize each other and the spike disappears. This enables us to run the process in reversed order, starting with a string along
{{\ell}}
, pull out a spike along
i
and stretch out the string to all three edges. We will refer to this reversed combination of moves as a
1\to 3
move because they transform one segment of the string into three.

If we start with a charge-neutral pointlike string and then extend it along one edge, then the wave function has to develop a Kroenecker delta as the string extends along this edge. This follows from the fact that this is the only
U(N)
gauge invariant tensor that is available of this form, together with the observation that we made around eq (
2.26
) for abelian gauge group that for a surface holonomy with vanishing area, we shall have a gauge invariant surface holonomy. We now elevate this to a general principle for both abelian and nonabelian gauge groups.

Let us now define a spike as any situation where two anti-parallel string segments coincide on one edge. With this definition of a spike we are ignoring how the spike may continue outside the spike-portion of the string and how it was created. It is not always true that the wave function of a spike will take the form of a Kroenecker delta since a spike on a string can arise in many other ways and does not have to originate from a charge-neutral pointlike string that is being pulled out over a vanishing surface area. For example if we parallel transport a regular string configuration on the lattice in a certain way, then a spike may develop as two segments of the string come together and meet on one edge. When such a spike is created there is no reason for the wave function to develop a Kroenecker delta function at the location of the spike. If we consider the
3\to 1
move, then we see that the relation

\displaystyle U^{{{\ell}}}{}_{i^{\prime}}{}^{j}{}_{k}\psi^{k}{}_{j}{}^{i}=c\psi^{{{\ell}}}\delta^{i}_{i^{\prime}}

(5.16)

is an example of this type. This relation does not necessarily have to hold in a generic situation since the spike that is produced here (on the edge with the color index
i
) was not obtained by a surface holonomy with vanishing area. However, we may assume that the relation above can hold if the conditions are calibrated carefully. We may calibrate the wave function by making sure that the
3\to 1
move follows right after we have made the
1\to 3
move, in which case the wave function has been calibrated though the
1\to 3
move.

This motivates us to refine our definition of a spike. We will refer to a spike portion of a string as a K-spike if it corresponds to a Kroenecker delta in that portion of the wave function of the string. A move that creates a K-spike will be referred to as a K-move. A move that removes the K-spike is referred to as an R-move. It is important to notice that we do not have a move that can remove a spike which is not a K-spike.

The Schrodinger wave function description appears to be consistent if we assign the rules that the wave function transforms as

\displaystyle\psi..._{j}{}^{k}...

\displaystyle\rightarrow

\displaystyle\psi..._{j}{}^{i}{}_{i^{\prime}}{}^{k}...=\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\delta^{i}_{i^{\prime}}\psi..._{j}{}^{k}...

(5.17)

when a K-spike is created on the string, and reversely as

\displaystyle\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\delta^{i}_{i^{\prime}}\psi..._{j}{}^{k}...

\displaystyle\rightarrow

\displaystyle\psi..._{j}{}^{k}...

(5.18)

when this K-spike is annihilated. In this description, we do not keep track of massless charge-neutral particles that may participate in the process since they can not be described by a nonrelativistic wave function. The wave function of the spike-portion of the string is given by
\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\delta^{i}_{i^{\prime}}
. The interpretation if we slightly separate the M5 branes is as follows. Firstly, this wave function then says that a string that goes out along
M5_{i}
can not annihilate a string that comes back along
M5_{i^{\prime}}
if
i^{\prime}\neq i
. This is the statement of charge conservation. Secondly, it says that the string goes out and comes back along the same
M5_{i}
brane with the probability
1/N
. We have a democratic probability distribution for the spike portion of the selfdual string to run out on anyone of these M5 branes. This assignment of giving equal probabilities corresponds for the case when these branes are coincident to the unique gauge invariant choice. Any other choice for these probabilities would not lead to a
U(N)
gauge invariant tensor
\sim\delta^{i}_{i^{\prime}}
. However, if we separate the M5 branes, then since we break the gauge symmetry we may have a different kind of wave function on the spike. Here we are however interested in the unbroken phase with
U(N)
gauge symmetry restored.

Let us now study how one closed string might be able to split into two separate strings. We draw such a process on a lattice as below,

a

(5.20)

The wave function transforms under these moves as follows,

\displaystyle\psi^{a}{}_{h}{}^{g}{}_{f}{}^{e}{}_{d}{}^{c}{}_{b}

\displaystyle\rightarrow

\displaystyle\psi^{a}{}_{h}{}^{g}{}_{i}{}^{b^{\prime}}{}_{j}{}^{e}{}_{d}{}^{c}{}_{b}=U_{i}{}^{b^{\prime}}{}_{j}{}^{f}\psi^{a}{}_{h}{}^{g}{}_{f}{}^{e}{}_{d}{}^{c}{}_{b}

(5.24)

The string may now split into two strings if it develops a K-spike that we can remove by an R-move,

\displaystyle\psi^{a}{}_{h}{}^{g}{}_{i}{}^{b^{\prime}}{}_{j}{}^{e}{}_{d}{}^{c}{}_{b}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle c\delta_{b}^{b^{\prime}}\psi^{a}{}_{h}{}^{g}{}_{i}\psi_{j}{}^{e}{}_{d}{}^{c}

(5.25)

\displaystyle\overset{\text{R-move}}{\longrightarrow}

\displaystyle\psi^{a}{}_{h}{}^{g}{}_{i}\psi_{j}{}^{e}{}_{d}{}^{c}

(5.26)

If the string does not develop the K-spike as the two distant segments of the string meet at the edge with the color indices
b
and
b^{\prime}
, then we need a different relativistic framework to describe that process.

Before any two segments come together and meet, our string is everywhere tensile, with every segment of the string having a mass and the Schrodinger wave function gives a good description of the string. As two segments of the string come together with opposite orientations on one edge of the lattice, what will happen is that the corresponding portion of the M2 brane will be annihilated. That is a very natural thing that we can expect, based on how we expect that two anti-parallel M2 branes annihilate into massless charge-neutral radiation particles. But now let us imagine that we separate our M5 branes slightly and that the M2 brane ends on
M5_{b}
and that the anti-M2 brane ends on
M5_{b^{\prime}}
where
b^{\prime}\neq b
. In that case, the annihilation process between the two M2 branes will not be perfect. A small portion will remain for one of these M2 branes that will be stretching between
M5_{b}
and
M5_{b^{\prime}}
. This will be percieved as very light string segment along the edge
b
from the perspective of the M5 brane theory. As we bring the M5 branes together it will become a massless string segment that we do not know how to describe with a nonrelativistic wave function. If on the other hand,
b=b^{\prime}
then the annihilation will be perfect, the segment will be annihilated and the string will split into two strings.

What happens if
b\neq b^{\prime}
as the two string segments meet on the same edge? To understand this, let us again slightly separate the M5 branes. Then we will see that the two strings will actually not meet on the same edge since they will reside on two different M5 branes, namely one resides on
M5_{b}
while the other on
M5_{b^{\prime}}
. So they can not annihilate into charge-neutral massless radiation particles. The string can not break because of charge conservation with respect to
U(1)_{b}
and
U(1)_{b^{\prime}}
separately. As we bring the M5 branes together and the
U(N)
gauge symmetry is restored, if we have a wave function that does not vanish for
b
and
b^{\prime}
different, then we seem to get a nonabelian charged tensionless string portion located on the edge
b
in the lattice. If the selfdual string could not break when the M5 branes where slightly separated by charge conservation, then it is unlikely that the string would be able to break as we bring the M5 branes on top of each other. We conclude that the string will not be able to break into two strings unless we get a K-spike on the edge
b
.

Let us now discuss the normalization of the wave function. The norm should be gauge invariant and observable. Gauge invariance means that we shall contract all the color indices when we form the norm of the wave function. Let us then analyze what happens to the norm under the string splitting process above. The norm square of the wave function, contracting all the color indices, becomes

\displaystyle c^{2}\delta_{b}^{b^{\prime}}\delta^{b}_{b^{\prime}}\left|\psi^{a}{}_{h}{}^{g}{}_{i}\psi_{j}{}^{e}{}_{d}{}^{c}\right|^{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle c^{2}N\left|\psi^{a}{}_{h}{}^{g}{}_{i}\psi_{j}{}^{e}{}_{d}{}^{c}\right|^{2}

(5.27)

We now see that if we pick the normalization constant as

\displaystyle c

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}

(5.28)

then we preserve the normalization of the wave function by the R-move. That means that the string still exists as a whole, with probability one, also after the R-move.

6
A string moving in the lattice

When the string moves over the lattice, it sweeps out a two-dimensional surface. Let us now focus on the case where this 2d surface is one plaquette in the hypercubic lattice. As a 2d surface, we may put an orientation on that surface, i.e. an orientation on the plaquette that the string is either going to sweep over, or has already swept over. Below we depict such a plaquette that participate specifically in such a 2d surface where we put an intrinsic orientation on it as indicated by the inner loop with an arrow pointing in one direction, which we refer to as ’the direction of the orientation’ of this plaquette,

U

We have placed the letter
U
in the middle of the plaquette. This letter represents the ’universal plaquette holonomy’. It is a unitary operator associated to this plaquette. This operator can transport a string across the plaquette in multiple different ways, which is why we refer to it as ’universal’.

Below we list the ways that a string that starts at the vertex with coordinate
x
and that are oriented along the plaquette can be transported to the other side

The other ’side’ refers here to the edges around the plaquette over which the string was not extended initially.

U

Therefore we will start with distinguishing between them by inserting a vertical line that separates the color indices into two groups. The indices that stand to the left of the vertical line correspond to the color indices of the transformed wave function. The indices that stand to the right of the vertical line are written in reversed order (which means reversed both in the left-right and the up-down directions) and they contract the indices of the original wave function.

All these moves, except for the
2\to 2
move, change the length of the string. We propose that the only possible way that the length can increase by a fundamental process is if two charges are created equal and opposite to each other on one edge. This is the process that we refer to as a K-spike move. Thus the first two moves, the
0\to 4
and the
1\to 3
moves, are actually composed of K-spike moves followed by a
2\to 2
move,

We need to calibrate here in order to avoid our string to get a tensionless portion that we do not understand how to analyze.

By comparing with (
6
) we get

\displaystyle U_{i}{}^{j}{}_{k}{}^{{{\ell}}}|

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle c^{2}U^{j}{}_{k}|{}^{{{\ell}}}{}_{i}

(6.21)

\displaystyle U^{j}{}_{k}{}^{{{\ell}}}|{}_{i}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle cU^{j}{}_{k}|{}^{{{\ell}}}{}_{i}

(6.22)

\displaystyle U^{{{\ell}}}|{}_{i}{}^{j}{}_{k}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{1}{cN}U^{{{\ell}}}{}_{i}|{}^{j}{}_{k}

(6.23)

\displaystyle U|{}_{i}{}^{j}{}_{k}{}^{{{\ell}}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{1}{c^{2}N^{2}}U^{{{\ell}}}{}_{i}|{}^{j}{}_{k}

(6.24)

and for the particular value
c=\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}
these relations become

\displaystyle U_{i}{}^{j}{}_{k}{}^{{{\ell}}}|

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{1}{N}U^{j}{}_{k}|{}^{{{\ell}}}{}_{i}

(6.25)

\displaystyle U^{j}{}_{k}{}^{{{\ell}}}|{}_{i}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}U^{j}{}_{k}|{}^{{{\ell}}}{}_{i}

(6.26)

\displaystyle U^{{{\ell}}}|{}_{i}{}^{j}{}_{k}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\sqrt{N}U^{{{\ell}}}{}_{i}|{}^{j}{}_{k}

(6.27)

\displaystyle U|{}_{i}{}^{j}{}_{k}{}^{{{\ell}}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle NU^{{{\ell}}}{}_{i}|{}^{j}{}_{k}

(6.28)

7
The
0\to 4
move and cyclicity

We will now examine the
0\to 4
move, under which the wave function transforms from that of a pointlike string at some vertex with coordinate
x
, to a string that goes around the entire plaquette,

\displaystyle\psi(x)\rightarrow\psi_{i}{}^{j}{}_{k}{}^{{{\ell}}}=U_{i}{}^{j}{}_{k}{}^{{{\ell}}}|\psi(x)

(7.1)

In order for the wave function
\psi_{i}{}^{j}{}_{k}{}^{{{\ell}}}
to match the symmetries of the string, it shall not depend on the choice of vertex from which the string was pulled out and it shall be cyclic symmetric

\displaystyle\psi{}_{i}{}^{j}{}_{k}{}^{{{\ell}}}=\psi{}^{{{\ell}}}{}_{i}{}^{j}{}_{k}=\psi{}_{k}{}^{{{\ell}}}{}_{i}{}^{j}=\psi{}^{j}{}_{k}{}^{{{\ell}}}{}_{i}

(7.2)

Let us now consider the fact that the same closed string that goes around the plaquette can be obtained by stretching out a pointlike string residing at anyone of the four vertices, as pictured below,

By moving a pointlike string from one vertex to another with spike-like holonomies we may derive the following equalities,

\displaystyle\psi(x)=\psi(y)=\psi(z)=\psi(w)

(7.8)

By further using the cyclicity of the string, we deduce that the
0\to 4
plaquette holonomy must be cyclic symmetric,

\displaystyle U_{i}{}^{j}{}_{k}{}^{{{\ell}}}|=U^{{{\ell}}}{}_{i}{}^{j}{}_{k}|=U_{k}{}^{{{\ell}}}{}_{i}{}^{j}|=U^{j}{}_{k}{}^{{{\ell}}}{}_{i}|

(7.9)

We are now at last ready to define our ’universal plaquette holonomy’ as

\displaystyle U_{i}{}^{j}{}_{k}{}^{{{\ell}}}

\displaystyle:=

\displaystyle NU_{i}{}^{j}{}_{k}{}^{{{\ell}}}|

(7.10)

The universal plaquette holonomy is cyclic symmetric,

\displaystyle U_{i}{}^{j}{}_{k}{}^{{{\ell}}}=U{}^{j}{}_{k}{}^{{{\ell}}}{}_{i}=U{}_{k}{}^{{{\ell}}}{}_{i}{}^{j}=U{}^{{{\ell}}}{}_{i}{}^{j}{}_{k}

(7.11)

8
Unitary compactness conditions

As a string moves in the lattice, it sweeps out a two-dimensional surface. To this surface we associate a surface holonomy. The string has an orientation. But in order to define the surface holonomy, we need to specify an orientation of the surface itself, independently of the orientation of the string that moves over the surface. Below we picture one plaquette that we assign an orientation as indicated by an inner black square with an arrow on it. We refer to this as the orientation of the surface, as opposed to the orientation of the string. Since there are two choices of this orientation, there are correspondingly, two kinds of surface holonomies that we denote by
U
and
\widetilde{U}
respectively. These are related as in the picture below,

(8.5)

For the wave function, this means that complex conjugation shall act as

\displaystyle\left(\psi_{i}{}^{j}{}_{k}{}^{{{\ell}}}\right)^{*}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\widetilde{\psi}_{{{\ell}}}{}^{k}{}_{j}{}^{i}

(8.6)

where we use tilde to emphasise that this can be some other wave function, which can be different from the original wave function. For a pointlike string residing in anyone of the four vertices, say at the vertex with the coordinate
x
, for which there are no color indices to specify its location, we will define

\displaystyle\psi(x)^{*}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\widetilde{\psi}(x)

(8.7)

For the pointlike string it becomes clear why we have introduced the tilte since we shall not require that the wave function for a pointlike string will have to be real-valued. This wave function can be complex-valued just as it is for any point-like object. This complex nature of the wave function does not necessarily imply that the particle carries
U(N)
charges (and the pointlike string does not). A complex-valued wave function can arise from some other charge under transportation, such as a discrete translational charge coupled to the particle. In the continuum spacetime this enables us to have a wave function that is a complex-valued plane wave. On the lattice, we do not have a plane wave. But we expect to have a discrete remnant of a plane wave. Therefore we shall allow for a complex-valued wave function for a pointlike string on the lattice.

Let us next assume that we have the
0\to 4
move under which these wave functions transform as

\displaystyle\psi(x)

\displaystyle\to

\displaystyle\psi_{i}{}^{j}{}_{k}{}^{{{\ell}}}=U_{i}{}^{j}{}_{k}{}^{{{\ell}}}\psi(x)

(8.8)

\displaystyle\widetilde{\psi}(x)

\displaystyle\to

\displaystyle\widetilde{\psi}_{{{\ell}}}{}^{k}{}_{j}{}^{i}=\widetilde{U}_{{{\ell}}}{}^{k}{}_{j}{}^{i}\widetilde{\psi}(x)

(8.9)

In the second line we use
\widetilde{U}
since the final string has the opposite orientation. By taking complex conjugation of the first relation, we discover a relation between
U
and
\widetilde{U}
. Namely, they are related by complex conjugation as

\displaystyle\widetilde{U}_{{{\ell}}}{}^{k}{}_{j}{}^{i}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\left(U_{i}{}^{j}{}_{k}{}^{{{\ell}}}\right)^{*}

(8.10)

We will now study the
2\to 2
move. We start with a string that goes along two edges of the plaquette, which are labeled by the color indices
i
and
j
. What the string does as it continues outside the plaquette to form a closed string in the end, is of no concern to us here. We will just assume that the string remains static outside the plaquette under consideration. We then move the string to the other side of the plaquette by a
2\to 2
move. It then stretches over the edges that carry the color indices
{{\ell}}
and
k
. Then we move the string back to its original position, but we will put primes on the color indices at this stage, so they will read
i^{\prime}
and
j^{\prime}
. The sequence of
2\to 2
movements is pictured below,

We have drawn the orientation of the surface along with the letter
U
to emphasise that
U
is defined with respect to this particular orientation. Since the string goes parallel with the orienation of the surface under the first move but antiparallel with the orientation of the surface under the second move, the wave function will transform differently under the two moves according to

\displaystyle\psi{}_{j}{}^{i}

\displaystyle\rightarrow

\displaystyle\psi{}_{k}{}^{{{\ell}}}=U{}_{k}{}^{{{\ell}}}{}_{i}{}^{j}\psi{}_{j}{}^{i}

(8.13)

\displaystyle\rightarrow

\displaystyle\psi{}_{j^{\prime}}{}^{i^{\prime}}=\widetilde{U}{}_{j^{\prime}}{}^{i^{\prime}}{}_{{{\ell}}}{}^{k}\psi{}_{k}{}^{{{\ell}}}=\widetilde{U}{}_{j^{\prime}}{}^{i^{\prime}}{}_{{{\ell}}}{}^{k}U{}_{k}{}^{{{\ell}}}{}_{i}{}^{j}\psi{}_{j}{}^{i}

(8.14)

As the string moves adiabatically over the plaquette and then back, it shall not changed as it comes back. This is the two-dimensional version of the zig-zag symmetry of a backtracking Wilson line in a Yang-Mills gauge theory. As this shall be true for an arbitrary initial wave function, we are led to the requirement that

\displaystyle\widetilde{U}{}_{j^{\prime}}{}^{i^{\prime}}{}_{{{\ell}}}{}^{k}U{}_{k}{}^{{{\ell}}}{}_{i}{}^{j}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\delta^{i^{\prime}}_{i}\delta_{j^{\prime}}^{j}

(8.15)

If we now recall the complex conjugation rule for the plaquette holonomy, then we can also write this condition as a unitary compactness condition,

\displaystyle\left(U{}_{k}{}^{{{\ell}}}{}_{i^{\prime}}{}^{j^{\prime}}\right)^{*}U{}_{k}{}^{{{\ell}}}{}_{i}{}^{j}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\delta^{i^{\prime}}_{i}\delta_{j^{\prime}}^{j}

(8.16)

We have introduced color indices with primes. This could seem to contradict our view that color indices serve as locations of edges in the lattice. However, we may still use indices as geometric locations of edges while attaching primes to distinguish their different values at that edge. So if we need to specify the edge
i
using two different strings, then we will denote these indices as
i
and
i^{\prime}
where both refer to the same edge in the lattice but where we allow for them to take two different index values, within the range
1,...,N
.

9
The
N^{2}
degrees of freedom in
U_{{{\ell}}}{}^{k}{}_{j}{}^{i}

The universal plaquette operator is represented as a tensor
U_{{{\ell}}}{}^{k}{}_{j}{}^{i}
. If we just consider this as an unconstrained tensor, then it will have
N^{4}
complex components. There is another version
U^{k}{}_{j}{}^{i}{}_{{{\ell}}}
with another set of
N^{4}
complex components. The conditions

\displaystyle U_{{{\ell}}}{}^{k}{}_{j}{}^{i}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle U^{k}{}_{j}{}^{i}{}_{{{\ell}}}

(9.1)

reduce this totality set of
2N^{4}
complex components to
N^{4}
complex components
\{U_{{{\ell}}}{}^{k}{}_{j}{}^{i}\}
. The reality conditions

\displaystyle\left(U_{{{\ell}}}{}^{k}{}_{j}{}^{i}\right)^{*}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\widetilde{U}_{i}{}^{j}{}_{k}{}^{{{\ell}}}

(9.2)

due to the tilde operator being independent, thus define another set of components and are thus still leaving us with
N^{4}
complex components. The symmetric conditions

\displaystyle U_{{{\ell}}}{}^{k}{}_{j}{}^{i}-U_{j}{}^{i}{}_{{{\ell}}}{}^{k}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle 0

(9.3)

comprise
N^{2}(N^{2}-1)/2
conditions which leave us with
N^{2}(N^{2}+1)/2
complex components. The unitarity conditions

\displaystyle\left(U_{{{\ell}}}{}^{k}{}_{j}{}^{i}\right)^{*}U_{{{\ell}}}{}^{k}{}_{j^{\prime}}{}^{i^{\prime}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\delta_{i}^{i^{\prime}}\delta_{j^{\prime}}^{j}

(9.4)

comprise
N^{4}
real conditions leaving us with

\displaystyle 2\frac{N^{2}\left(N^{2}+1\right)}{2}-N^{4}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle N^{2}

(9.5)

real components in the universal plaquette operator at the end of the day.

10
The unit plaquette operator

In this section we will discuss the unit plaquette operator that we will denote as
{\cal{I}}_{i}{}^{j}{}_{k}{}^{{{\ell}}}
. Obviously it shall be cyclically symmetric and unitary,

\displaystyle{\cal{I}}_{i}{}^{j}{}_{k}{}^{{{\ell}}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle{\cal{I}}^{j}{}_{k}{}^{{{\ell}}}{}_{i}

(10.1)

\displaystyle\left({\cal{I}}_{i}{}^{j}{}_{k}{}^{{{\ell}}}\right)^{*}{\cal{I}}_{i}{}^{j}{}_{a}{}^{b}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\delta_{a}^{k}\delta^{b}_{{{\ell}}}

(10.2)

just as any universal plaquette operator. One may then try some Kroenecker combinations and check whether they can satisfy both these conditions. The obvious guess would be to take the
U(N)
invariant combination
\delta_{i}^{j}\delta_{k}^{{{\ell}}}+\delta_{i}^{{{\ell}}}\delta^{j}_{k}
which is cyclically symmetric. But this does not satisfy the unitary constraint. Instead, we find that a solution that satisfies both the cyclicity and unitarity constraints is of the form

\displaystyle{\cal{I}}_{i}{}^{j}{}_{k}{}^{{{\ell}}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle S_{ik}S^{j{{\ell}}}

(10.3)

where
S_{ij}
is any symmetric and unitary matrix,

\displaystyle S_{ij}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle S_{ji}

(10.4)

\displaystyle\left(S_{ij}\right)^{*}S_{jk}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\delta^{i}_{k}

(10.5)

We define

\displaystyle S^{ij}

\displaystyle:=

\displaystyle\left(S_{ij}\right)^{*}

(10.6)

We claim that this is the best candidate for a unit plaquette operator that we can possibly find. It is not uniquely defined, it can not be since there is no invariant tensor
S_{ij}
in the
U(N)
gauge group. Thus our claim must be that any solution
S_{ij}
works equally well for defining the unit.

We will now show in what sense this plaquette operator can act like a unit. To this end, we will lift a closed string that goes around a plaquette in the basement floor up to the first floor, and then up to the second floor. Why we need to lift the string all the way up to the second floor is related to the bipartite structure of the lattice. The process of lifting the string two floors up is shown below,

We may think on the process as follows. We start by the first and in some sense the most heavy lift where we lift the string segment
{{\ell}}
by a
1\to 3
move. This is implemented by acting with

\displaystyle c{\cal{I}}_{{{\ell}}}{}^{f}{}_{d}{}^{e}

(10.9)

We tend to think on this lift as heavy since we need to lift three segments. After that has been done, the subsequent lifts are in some sense no so heavy as they only require us to lift two segments using the
2\to 2
moves that we use to lift up the string segments
k
,
j
and
i
in turn by acting with

\displaystyle{\cal{I}}^{i}{}_{e^{\prime}}{}^{a}{}_{h}{\cal{I}}_{j}{}^{h}{}_{b}{}^{g}{\cal{I}}^{k}{}_{g}{}^{c}{}_{f}

(10.10)

Now when we make the last lift job, that is by acting with
{\cal{I}}^{i}{}_{e}{}^{a}{}_{h}
, which is lifting up the segment
i
, we discover that the edge
e
is already occupied by the string. Namely, it is occupied by the string that was lifted up with the initial and heaviest
1\to 3
move. That means we shall put a prime for the color index
e
for this final
2\to 2
move as
{\cal{I}}^{i}{}_{e^{\prime}}{}^{a}{}_{h}
. The wave function of the string under this lift will transform as

\displaystyle(\psi_{1})_{e^{\prime}}{}^{a}{}_{b}{}^{c}{}_{d}{}^{e}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle c{\cal{I}}^{i}{}_{e^{\prime}}{}^{a}{}_{h}{\cal{I}}_{j}{}^{h}{}_{b}{}^{g}{\cal{I}}^{k}{}_{g}{}^{c}{}_{f}{\cal{I}}_{{{\ell}}}{}^{f}{}_{d}{}^{e}(\psi_{0})_{i}{}^{j}{}_{k}{}^{{{\ell}}}

(10.11)

If we plug in our expression for the unit, we get

\displaystyle(\psi_{1})_{e^{\prime}}{}^{a}{}_{b}{}^{c}{}_{d}{}^{e}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle c\delta^{e}_{e^{\prime}}S^{ai}S_{bj}S^{ck}S_{d{{\ell}}}(\psi_{0})_{i}{}^{j}{}_{k}{}^{{{\ell}}}

(10.12)

The wave function on the left-hand side has two segments on the same edge. In order to be able to proceed, then in this situation we usually assume that a K-spike is obtained on the edge where a spike is formed. But here we see that a K-spike forms automatically although these surface holonomies cover a nonvanishing surface area. The appearance of a K-spike where two segments coincide appears to be somehow encoded in the unit plaquette operators. Let us now prepare for the spike-removal move, the R-move, by defining

\displaystyle(\psi_{1})_{e^{\prime}}{}^{a}{}_{b}{}^{c}{}_{d}{}^{e}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle c\delta_{e^{\prime}}^{e}(\psi_{1})^{a}{}_{b}{}^{c}{}_{d}

(10.13)

and then we find, after the R-move, that the wave function transforms as

\displaystyle(\psi_{1})^{a}{}_{b}{}^{c}{}_{d}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle S^{ai}S_{bj}S^{ck}S_{d{{\ell}}}(\psi_{0})_{i}{}^{j}{}_{k}{}^{{{\ell}}}

(10.14)

We can now iterate the process one more time and lift the string up to the second floor. Repeating the full procedure once more, that is, first the heavy
1\to 3
move, followed by three
2\to 2
moves and finally an R-move of an assumed K-spike, the wave function transforms as

\displaystyle(\psi_{2})_{m}{}^{n}{}_{p}{}^{q}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle S_{ma}S^{nb}S_{pc}S^{qd}(\psi_{1})^{a}{}_{b}{}^{c}{}_{d}

(10.15)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\left(S_{ma}S^{nb}S_{pc}S^{qd}\right)\left(S^{ai}S_{bj}S^{ck}S_{d{{\ell}}}\right)(\psi_{0})_{i}{}^{j}{}_{k}{}^{{{\ell}}}

(10.16)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle(\psi_{0})_{m}{}^{n}{}_{p}{}^{q}

(10.17)

We now see that we indeed moved to the second floor without any change, thus justifying the name of ’unit’ for our plaquette operator
{\cal{I}}_{i}{}^{j}{}_{k}{}^{{{\ell}}}
.

Admittedly, we had to calibrate at one step in order to generate a K-spike. That means that this operator acts like a unit in situations where we can carry out the computation. That is of course as much as we should ask for. It would be rather pointless the ask if this operator still would act like a unit in a regime where we can not compute anything. In that regime we need a completely different computational framework and we expect everything to change to such a degree that nothing of what we do here can be carried over to that regime where we may have some sort of tensionless strings.

Let us briefly comment on other possible uses of the unit. The most basic move one may think of is that of stretching out a right-angled two-spike string so that it goes around one plaquette.

\lxSVG@closescope {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}}}&\begin{array}[]{cc}&\psi{}_{i}{}^{j^{\prime}}{}_{k^{\prime}}{}^{{{\ell}}}=c^{2}\delta_{i}^{j^{\prime}}\delta^{{{\ell}}}_{k^{\prime}}\psi(x)\cr&\rightarrow\psi_{i}{}^{j}{}_{k}{}^{{{\ell}}}={\cal{I}}^{j}{}_{k}{}^{k^{\prime}}{}_{j^{\prime}}\psi{}_{i}{}^{j^{\prime}}{}_{k^{\prime}}{}^{{{\ell}}}\cr&=c^{2}{\cal{I}}^{j}{}_{k}{}^{{{\ell}}}{}_{i}\psi(x)\end{array}\end{array}

The spike-string wave function is given by

\displaystyle\psi{}_{i}{}^{j^{\prime}}{}_{k^{\prime}}{}^{{{\ell}}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle c^{2}\delta_{i}^{j^{\prime}}\delta^{{{\ell}}}_{k^{\prime}}\psi(x)

(10.23)

We then stretch out the segments
j^{\prime}
and
k^{\prime}
by the unit, which transforms the wave function as

\displaystyle\psi{}_{i}{}^{j^{\prime}}{}_{k^{\prime}}{}^{{{\ell}}}\to\psi_{i}{}^{j}{}_{k}{}^{{{\ell}}}=c^{2}{\cal{I}}^{j}{}_{k}{}^{{{\ell}}}{}_{i}\psi(x)=c^{2}S_{{{\ell}}j}S^{ki}\psi(x)

(10.24)

The transformed wave function
c^{2}S_{{{\ell}}j}S^{ki}\psi(x)
is not the same as the spike-string wave function
c^{2}\delta_{i}^{j^{\prime}}\delta^{{{\ell}}}_{k^{\prime}}\psi(x)
that we started with. But that could not be expected because the two string configurations are completely different from one another. The unit can be made to act like a unit only when it acts on things that we can equate. Specifically, it can be made to act like a unit when the initial and the final string configurations are exactly the same when embedded in the lattice and indistinguishable from each other up to translation and rotation.

Now having this unit, we may expand around it as

\displaystyle U_{i}{}^{j}{}_{k}{}^{{{\ell}}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle{\cal{I}}_{i}{}^{j}{}_{k}{}^{{{\ell}}}+ieT_{i}{}^{j}{}_{k}{}^{{{\ell}}}+{\cal{O}}(e^{2})

(10.25)

and in this way study the set-up perturbatively in the dimensionless parameter
e
. This is not possible for a selfdual string for which
e
is fixed at its selfdual value. But if our string is not magnetically charged, then
e
can be choosen arbitrarily small and it can then serve as an expansion parameter. Unitarity implies that

\displaystyle\left(T_{i}{}^{j}{}_{k}{}^{{{\ell}}}\right)^{*}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle T_{{{\ell}}}{}^{k}{}_{j}{}^{i}

(10.26)

An interesting explicit realization that also satisfies the cyclic condition is given by

\displaystyle U_{i}{}^{j}{}_{k}{}^{{{\ell}}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle{\cal{I}}_{i}{}^{j}{}_{k}{}^{{{\ell}}}+ie\left(S_{ij}P^{k{{\ell}}}+P_{ij}S^{k{{\ell}}}\right)+{\cal{O}}(e^{2})

(10.27)

where
(P_{ij})^{*}=P^{ij}
and
P_{ij}=P_{ji}
but which is otherwise an unconstrained matrix that captures
{\cal{O}}(N^{2})
degrees of freedom of the plaquette holonomy.

11
The disallowed spike moves

Let us consider a string that wraps around four edges of one plaquette, and then let us try to pull out a spike from one of its vertices
x
, such that the spike runs parallel with the edge
i
in the plaquette. After that, we apply a
2\to 2
move. These moves are pictured below,

(11.1)

Under the first spike-move from
x
the wave function transforms as

\displaystyle\psi{}_{{{\ell}}}{}^{k}{}_{j}{}^{i}\rightarrow c\delta^{i^{\prime\prime}}_{i^{\prime}}\psi{}_{{{\ell}}}{}^{k}{}_{j}{}^{i}

(11.2)

A K-spike is generated here since the surface holonomy that creates this spike has vanishing area by pulling out a spike from the vertex
x
. Hence this surface holonomy needs to be an
U(N)
invariant and therefore the K-spike is the only possibility. However, we could get the same string configuration if instead we pull out a spike from
y
, in which case the wave function transforms as

\displaystyle\psi{}_{{{\ell}}}{}^{k}{}_{j}{}^{i}\rightarrow c\delta^{i}_{i^{\prime}}\psi{}_{{{\ell}}}{}^{k}{}_{j}{}^{i^{\prime\prime}}

(11.3)

By the uniqueness of the wave function, we can not have two different wave functions assigned to this same graph. We conclude that creating a K-spike on an edge that is already occupied by a string is disallowed. From this it follows that it is disallowed to have three spikes in one plaquette, as it was created from a disallowed string configuration in the second move in (
11.1
). However, there is no limit on how many spikes that a string can have as long as no more than two spikes are located on one plaquette.

(11.7)

What seems to happen as we try pull the string out from the vertex
z
, is that the string wants to minimize its total length. As we try to pull out a spike from the vertex
z
, the string will find the other allowed configuration that costs less energy as that allowed configuration only requires four string segments instead of six for the disallowed configuration.

12
The Wilson surface of a cube

We will now obtain an expression for the Wilson surface of a cube by ’lassoing’ the cube. Below is a picture of the cube where on each face we have put a roman letter. We use the letters
A,B,C,a,b,c
to denote the universal plaquette operator on each face.

a
A
b
B
c
C

As a two-dimensional surface, it has an intrinsic orientation. The orientation is represented by an arrow of closed loops drawn on the surface. In the picture we have drawn a few such loops. There are two choices for the direction of the arrow and hence of the orientation of the surface. Once we pick an orientation of one loop, then the orientation of all the other loops on the surface is uniquely fixed by requiring that the arrows of any two loops that meet at a point have arrows that are anti-parallel.

Now we also like to put the color indices on the edges. Therefore we will draw the same cube again, this time with color indices on the edges,

{{\ell}}
k
j
i
h
g
f
d
c
b
a
e

Now we shall pull a closed string over the cube. We may imagine that we shall throw out a lasso from some base point and then wrap the lasso around the entire cube and then pull back the lasso to the base point again. There are various ways that one can do this. One way is as pictured in the sequence below, where the base point is the vertex at which the string starts out as a pointlike string,
